On screenawaiting-confirmation195.2s
You
Target the ones who have never started a request — customers with an eligible outstanding balance who haven't raised an OS-to-EMI request at all.
Agent
Target active-account customers approaching their statement due date with a short, escalating-channel reminder sequence that surfaces the OS-to-EMI option, since they confirmed acquisition (never-started) is the target and due-date timing is their own urgency hypothesis. Because the platform cannot filter by outstanding balance or by 'has never raised a request', the buildable audience is broader than the one they described — this is surfaced below, not hidden. The cost-hesitation belief is tested, not assumed, via a two-arm message-angle experiment with a holdout to read any incremental effect honestly.
Approach
  • Audience = acquisition only (never-started), per the user's explicit, twice-confirmed answer — basis: user.
  • Entry built as an audience filter on Account (Status = Active, Statement Due Date near the upcoming cycle) because no event exists for 'became eligible for OS-to-EMI' and no attribute proves 'has never raised a request' — basis: tool (list_audience_attributes/list_event_types), trade-off stated below.
  • Balance threshold (>₹25,000) left unbuilt rather than approximated with Transaction Amount, because that attribute is a single transaction's value, not a running outstanding balance — basis: tool, decision: do not substitute.
  • Goal = EMI Request New Status Equals Successful, Source Equals OS-to-EMI — basis: tool (list_audience_attributes confirms this exact Source value and status list exist).
  • Cost-hesitation belief treated as a hypothesis under test, not a given, via an A/B on the opening message's angle (cost-reassurance vs. simplicity/awareness) with reminders held identical across arms so only one variable changes — basis: own judgement, applying P-005 (change one variable per experiment).
  • Channel order EMAIL → SMS → WHATSAPP, cheapest first, escalating for reminders — basis: tenant preference (prefer lower-cost channel first) and P-010.
  • 3 messages total (within the 4-message cap), 48h minimum spacing — basis: tool/knowledge-base hard constraints.
  • 10% control holdout — basis: tenant preference, applied because any read of 'more requests reaching Successful' as campaign-attributable needs a no-message comparison (P-006).
Options weighed
  • Segmentation — used. Message-angle segmentation (cost-reassurance vs. simplicity) is built via experiment arms; balance-based segmentation is the user's stated hunch but cannot be built — no balance attribute exists, so it is not used for targeting, only recorded as an open hypothesis.
  • Experimentation — used. Competing explanations for non-conversion (cost hesitation vs. general awareness/friction) are real and the user cannot know which dominates, so a 50/50 single-variable angle test on the opening message is run, read against requests reaching Successful per arm.
  • Conditional branching — not applicable here. The only branch that matters here — did the customer convert — is already handled automatically by the platform's goal-check/exit after every send and wait (P-008). The builder's condition step only reads a previous send's delivery outcome, which doesn't carry conversion information, so no additional branch adds value.
  • Channel fallback — not applicable here. Not something this business case leans on, and also not expressible: the builder documentation states a fallback channel on a send cannot be configured here. Sequential multi-channel reminders (EMAIL then SMS then WHATSAPP) partly cover the same need by design, not as an automatic retry.
  • Adaptive sequencing — used. Channel escalates from cheapest (EMAIL) to richer channels (SMS, WHATSAPP) as reminders progress, and the whole entry window is anchored to statement-due-date proximity per the user's urgency hunch.
  • Cost and fatigue — used. Capped at 3 of the allowed 4 messages, 48h minimum spacing. Weakest message is the third (WhatsApp, higher relative cost): kept because it is the only touch that lands closest to the due date when urgency is hypothesised to be highest, but it is the first candidate to cut if fatigue or low engagement is observed.
  • Measurement and learning — used. 10% holdout lets the business separate campaign-attributable effect from background conversion; the angle experiment lets them learn which framing (cost vs. simplicity) moves EMI Requests to Successful, without claiming a lift number up front.
Considered and not used
  • Delay launch until a balance-threshold data feed exists and run a precision-targeted campaign instead — Conservative risk appetite favours well-targeted messaging, but the user set no fixed target and the behaviour (never having started a request) is time-sensitive relative to each statement cycle. Launching now on the broader active-account audience, with the gap stated plainly, is preferred over an indefinite delay — but this is a trade-off the user should confirm, not one made silently.
Success criteria
  • No fixed numeric target was set. The business's own measure, as given: success is more EMI Requests reaching Successful (Source = OS-to-EMI) — a directional read, not a target rate or lift figure.
Measurement
  • Track count and rate of EMI Request New Status = Successful (Source = OS-to-EMI) among campaign entrants versus the 10% holdout, to read an incremental difference rather than an absolute count.
  • Track the same outcome split by experiment arm (cost-reassurance opening vs. simplicity/awareness opening) to learn which framing the interest-cost hesitation belief actually explains, if either.
  • Track Pending/Failed/Expired EMI Request volumes per arm as a secondary signal of flow friction (requests started but not completed) versus never-started behaviour.
  • To measure properly: a precomputed 'never raised an OS-to-EMI request' flag and a running outstanding-balance figure per customer, refreshed per statement cycle, would let targeting and later analysis match what the business actually asked for.
Assumptions
  • Account Status = Active is an adequate proxy for 'account still open and not closed/charge-off/suspended', used as a baseline eligibility filter since no explicit NPA flag is exposed in this attribute list.
  • The exact Statement Due Date window ('near due date') will be configured at build/run time per statement cycle; proposed default is 7 days before due date.
  • Quiet hours and DNC/NPA exclusion are enforced by the platform's send layer, not by this blueprint's conditions.
Hypotheses for future testing
  • Interest-cost hesitation is a primary barrier to starting an OS-to-EMI request (user's belief, under test via message angle).
  • Proximity to the statement due date raises receptiveness to an OS-to-EMI offer (user's belief, applied as entry timing, not separately tested here).
  • Outstanding balances above ₹25,000 convert at a different rate than smaller balances (user's belief; cannot be tested without a balance attribute — flagged as an evidence gap for a future data feed).
Worth settling before this is built
  • The buildable audience (active accounts near their statement due date) cannot exclude customers who already have an open or completed OS-to-EMI request, because no attribute proves 'has never raised a request' and the builder has no cross-entity exclusion filter. This means some customers who already converted, or who already have a Pending/Failed/Expired request, will still receive the first message as if they had never started one. Do you want to accept this overlap for launch, or hold until a precomputed 'never started OS-to-EMI' flag can be supplied? This determines who actually receives message 1 — someone who already has a pending request reading 'you haven't started yet' looks careless, not helpful, and is the kind of wrong-audience outcome that should be decided by the business, not absorbed silently. Until then: Launch on the Account-level audience as specified; rely only on the platform's automatic goal-check (which exits anyone who reaches Successful after their first touchpoint) to limit further messaging, accepting that the very first send may still reach some already-engaged customers.
  • The >₹25,000 outstanding-balance threshold cannot be built with any attribute currently exposed (no running-balance field exists on Account or Customer; Transaction Amount is per-transaction). Can you supply a precomputed segment or smart-tag flag carrying this threshold, or should the campaign proceed without it? Without it, the campaign reaches all eligible active accounts regardless of balance size, which is a materially different and broader audience than the one your hunch describes. Until then: Proceed without the balance filter; the campaign reaches the full active-account population near their due date, not just the >₹25,000 segment.
Limitations
  • EMI Events is marked new in the platform metadata: proposed, not confirmed as built in production. This campaign depends on it, so it cannot be presented as a verified platform capability.
  • Transaction Events and EMI Events (which the goal depends on) are both marked 'new — proposed, not confirmed built in production' by the platform metadata. If EMI_STATUS_CHANGED is not actually live, the goal cannot fire and the campaign cannot measure Successful conversions at all.
  • Per-send channel fallback on delivery failure is not expressible in this builder. A failed EMAIL send will not automatically retry on SMS; the customer simply misses that touch unless a later scheduled send reaches them.

You
I want to increase OS-to-EMI conversions. Design a drip campaign for this.
Agent
I checked the platform's event vocabulary, audience attributes, channels and template availability. 'EMI Request' has a Source value literally called 'OS-to-EMI', with a New Status of Pending, Successful, Failed, Expired or Cancelled — so the platform can see an OS-to-EMI request's lifecycle. But that reveals a real fork before I can design anything: 'OS-to-EMI conversion' could mean two different behaviours. (1) A customer has already started an OS-to-EMI request (it sits at New Status = Pending) and needs to be nudged to finish it before it lapses — P-003 says these stay open up to 7 days before Expiring. (2) A customer has an outstanding balance eligible for OS-to-EMI but has never started a request at all, and needs to be prompted to begin one. These need different entry events, different audiences, and different messages (finish-what-you-started vs. here's-an-option-you-have), so I can't pick one for you. I also need the business's own definition of success before I design the measurement, per the brief, and I want to know what you believe is actually stopping people from converting, since that changes what the messages say (and whether one message can address it or I should test competing explanations).
1How do you want success judged for this campaign — e.g. completion rate of OS-to-EMI requests, a reduction in requests that expire unconverted, growth in new requests started, or something else you already track? If there's no target yet, say so and I'll record it as not yet set.
2Should this campaign target customers who already have a Pending OS-to-EMI request and need to finish it before it expires, or customers who have an eligible outstanding balance but haven't started a request yet and need to be told the option exists? (Or both, as two separate tracks?)
3What do you believe is the main reason customers don't complete OS-to-EMI — e.g. they're put off by the interest/fee, they don't understand the option, the request process has too many steps, or they simply forget? If you're not sure, say so and I'll treat it as an open question rather than guess.

On screenawaiting-confirmation266.3s
You
Target the ones who have never started a request — customers with an eligible outstanding balance who haven't raised an OS-to-EMI request at all.
Agent
Target active accounts and prompt the OS-to-EMI option to customers who have never raised a request, since no eligibility or balance field exists to narrow this further. Run a controlled test of cost-reassurance messaging against plain awareness messaging, since the user's 'interest-cost hesitation' belief is unverified and the two framings lead to materially different copy. Hold out a control group so any observed difference in Successful conversions can be read against what would have happened anyway. Keep the sequence to three touches to respect the message cap and avoid fatiguing an audience whose eligibility can't be confirmed.
Approach
  • Entry on Account Status = Active (tool: this is the only attribute on an entity related to 'eligibility' that the builder exposes; it is a proxy for 'in good standing', not for 'has an eligible outstanding balance' — that field does not exist) — assumption, clearly weaker than the user's intended criterion.
  • Goal = EMI Request New Status Equals 'Successful' AND Source Equals 'OS-to-EMI' (tool: EMI Request exposes exactly this status/source combination) — matches the user's own definition of success.
  • Message framing run as an A/B experiment (cost-reassurance vs plain nudge) instead of picking one reading of the user's belief — decision made because the user cannot know which barrier dominates and a controlled comparison can tell us, per user-belief handling rule.
  • No entry filter on Statement Due Date — this tool interface cannot confirm a safe way to express a rolling per-customer date window as a condition; encoding a fixed date would apply the wrong window to everyone. Due-date urgency is carried as an unbuilt intent, not faked with a static date (assumption, mine).
  • Three sends per customer, not four — cost-and-fatigue judgement: a fourth generic reminder adds marginal reach against an audience that is unfiltered on eligibility, so the risk of irritating someone to whom the message may not even apply outweighs the small extra chance of conversion (my judgement, no data to size this).
  • Channel order EMAIL → SMS → WHATSAPP, cheapest-first (tool: list_channels cost order; tenant preference 'prefer lower-cost channel first').
Options weighed
  • Segmentation — used. Split by message framing (cost-reassurance vs plain nudge) via experiment arms, since the barrier belief is contested. Could not segment by balance size as the user hypothesised — no attribute exists.
  • Experimentation — used. Controlled comparison of cost-reassurance vs plain-nudge first touch, same structure and timing otherwise, so any observed gap in reaching 'Successful' is attributable to framing, not asserted as a known lift.
  • Conditional branching — cannot evaluate yet. A SPLIT/condition step routes one way with no confirmed rejoin back to the main path (tool: list_step_types marks it routesOneWay). Branching on delivery outcome to add a manual channel-fallback would either duplicate the whole downstream sequence in both arms or silently drop customers on one side. I'd need to confirm rejoin behaviour before using it safely, so I left the journey single-line instead of guessing.
  • Channel fallback — not applicable here. No native per-send fallback exists in this builder interface (explicitly listed as unsupported), and the condition-based workaround is the 'cannot-evaluate' item above. Noted as an operational limitation rather than built around with an untested workaround.
  • Adaptive sequencing — used. Sequence is ordered to reinforce near the statement cycle conceptually (first-touch awareness, mid reminder, final nudge), though not anchored to each customer's own due date for the reason above — a partial, not full, implementation of the adaptive idea.
  • Cost and fatigue — used. Capped at 3 sends against a 4-message/48h-spacing limit; the weakest candidate message was a 4th generic reminder, cut because it adds fatigue risk to an audience of unconfirmed eligibility for a small, unsized marginal gain.
  • Measurement and learning — used. 10% control group held out (tenant preference) so any gap in Successful-conversion rate between treated and untreated, and between the two framings, can be read as a comparison rather than claimed as caused.
Considered and not used
  • Focus the campaign on recovering Pending OS-to-EMI requests before their 7-day expiry (the cleanly buildable track), instead of or alongside the not-started track — The user explicitly chose to target not-started customers. The Pending-recovery track remains fully buildable today (EMI Request Source='OS-to-EMI', New Status='Pending', with a known 7-day expiry per P-003) and is a materially different, more precisely targeted campaign. Recommend considering it as a second, separate track since it reaches a confirmed in-flight audience rather than an unfiltered one.
Success criteria
  • Business's own measure (no fixed target): more EMI Requests reaching New Status = Successful (Source = OS-to-EMI) among those who were targeted.
Measurement
  • Primary: count and rate of entrants whose EMI Request reaches New Status = Successful (Source = OS-to-EMI), read against the 10% control group — never claimed as caused without that comparison.
  • Secondary/leading indicator: rate of entrants whose EMI Request reaches New Status = Pending at all (i.e. they started one), since 'Successful' alone won't show whether the message got someone to begin — note EMI_STATUS_CHANGED is tool-flagged as 'new / proposed, not confirmed built in production', so this secondary measure depends on that event actually existing.
  • Split every measure by experiment arm (cost-reassurance vs plain nudge) to learn which framing the audience responds to, rather than assuming the user's cost-hesitation belief.
  • To measure properly would need: a confirmed outstanding-balance field (to test the ₹25,000 hunch), a confirmed 'became eligible' event (to size and time the true audience), and the EMI_STATUS_CHANGED event's production status confirmed.
Assumptions
  • Account Status = Active is the best available stand-in for 'in good standing'; it is not an eligibility or balance filter.
  • 48-hour spacing (platform minimum) is acceptable between all three sends; could be widened for the final message as a lower-fatigue trade-off.
  • DNC and NPA exclusion are enforced by the platform as standing guardrails, not re-specified here.
  • The goal check's automatic exit will stop messaging anyone who reaches 'Successful' after their first touch, which partially (not fully) offsets the risk of messaging someone who already converted before entry.
Hypotheses for future testing
  • A cost-reassurance framing (showing interest/payable upfront) will out-convert a plain awareness nudge for this audience — untested.
  • Messaging timed near the statement due date increases response — untested here since due-date timing could not be safely operationalised as an entry filter from this interface.
  • Customers with outstanding balances above ₹25,000 convert better — untested and currently unmeasurable with available fields.
Worth settling before this is built
  • This audience (Account Status = Active) cannot be made to exclude customers who already hold any OS-to-EMI EMI Request — Pending, Successful, Failed or Cancelled — because entry conditions can only filter one entity and the builder has no cross-entity exclusion. Some customers who have already started, or already completed, an OS-to-EMI conversion could receive a 'you can convert your balance' message. Do you want to accept that risk as scoped, or hold the campaign until a suppression mechanism exists? This is not an implementation footnote — real customers who already acted would be told to do something they've already done, which is confusing and a poor experience, and it dilutes the true 'never started' population the user asked for. Until then: Proceed as scoped against Account Status = Active only. The automatic goal-check will stop messaging anyone whose request reaches Successful after their first touch, which partially limits (but does not prevent) the overlap for Pending/Failed/Cancelled requesters.
Defaults applied
  • Spacing between the three sends is set to the 48-hour platform minimum. Tighter spacing reaches people faster but risks more fatigue; wider spacing is gentler but slower, which matters less here since due-date timing isn't precisely anchored anyway. Until then: Keep 48-hour spacing between all three sends.
Limitations
  • EMI Events is marked new in the platform metadata: proposed, not confirmed as built in production. This campaign depends on it, so it cannot be presented as a verified platform capability.
  • The ₹25,000 outstanding-balance hunch cannot be used to filter the audience — no attribute on Account, EMI Request or Transaction represents a running outstanding balance. The campaign will reach all active accounts, not just higher-balance ones. The audience actually reached is broader than the one the user hypothesised converts better; relevance (and likely response) may be lower than if it could be narrowed.
  • Account and Card both expose a 'Smart Tag' attribute that is issuer-configured, but this tool cannot see what tag values actually exist for this tenant. It's possible an eligibility-style tag already exists that would meaningfully tighten this audience. If such a tag exists, it could close part of the balance/eligibility gap above without waiting for a new field to be built.
  • Statement Due Date exists as an Account attribute, but this interface gives no confirmed way to express a reliable rolling per-customer window (e.g. 'due in the next 7 days') as an entry condition. The user's 'urgency rises near the due date' hunch cannot be operationalised as a targeting/timing filter here, so the sequence's timing is generic rather than anchored to each customer's own cycle.

Blueprint behind the confirm button

OS-to-EMI Awareness Drip — Not-Yet-Started Customers · control 10%

Prompts active-account customers who have not raised an OS-to-EMI request to consider converting their outstanding balance to EMI, testing cost-reassurance framing against a plain awareness framing, with a held-out control group.

entry: {"kind": "audience", "entity": "Account", "conditions": [{"attribute": "Status", "operator": "Equals", "value": "Active"}]}
goal : {"eventCategory": "EMI Events", "eventType": "EMI_STATUS_CHANGED", "conditions": [{"attribute": "New Status", "operator": "Equals", "value": "Successful"}, {"attribute": "Source", "operator": "Equals", "value": "OS-to-EMI"}]}
  1. EXPERIMENT

On screendiscovery42.7s
You
I want to increase OS-to-EMI conversions. Design a drip campaign for this.
Agent
I've confirmed the platform has a real OS-to-EMI vocabulary: EMI Request has Source="OS-to-EMI" and Product Type="Outstanding", with New Status values Pending/Successful/Failed/Expired/Cancelled, so a goal and entry can genuinely be built on this behaviour rather than approximated. Before designing I need two things only the business can give: how success will be judged, and which point in the OS-to-EMI journey this campaign should target — because 'OS-to-EMI conversion' could mean two different behaviours with two different audiences: (a) customers who are eligible to convert an outstanding balance to EMI but have never started a request, or (b) customers who started an OS-to-EMI request (New Status=Pending) but haven't completed it before it expires (per P-003, these auto-expire after 7 days). These lead to different entry events, different messages, and different urgency — so I want this settled before proposing rather than guessing. I also want your read on why customers aren't converting, since that drives the message mechanism (cost/interest concern vs. unawareness vs. a stalled request), and that's a belief only you can offer.
1How do you want success judged for this campaign — e.g. number/value of outstanding balances converted to EMI, a conversion rate off a defined eligible base, or something else? If you don't have a target yet, say so and I'll use a working measure and flag it as mine.
2Should this campaign target customers who are eligible but haven't started an OS-to-EMI request yet, customers who started one but haven't completed it (which expires after 7 days), or both as separate tracks?
3What do you believe is actually stopping customers from converting — e.g. the interest cost, not knowing the option exists, finding the request flow confusing, or something else? If you're not sure, that's useful to know too.

    why The mechanism of the message — surfacing a benefit, explaining cost, or simply reminding — depends on what's actually blocking the customer. A broad 'hesitation' answer would still need narrowing to one of these before the copy can be written with intent.

    why A customer with a large revolving balance may warrant a different urgency or channel than one with a small balance; whether this matters enough to segment is a business call, not something I should assume.

On screenawaiting-confirmation201.2s
You
No fixed target — success is more EMI Requests reaching Successful. Our hunch is that outstanding balances above 25,000 rupees convert better, and that urgency rises near the statement due date. We think interest-cost hesitation is the barrier.
Agent
Target customers whose OS-to-EMI request is sitting Pending, and drive them to Successful before the request auto-expires in 7 days (P-003). Because the stated barrier (interest-cost hesitation) is a belief, not a confirmed finding, the opening message is A/B tested between a cost-clarity framing and a simplicity framing, with a 10% holdout so any observed difference isn't mistaken for proof of lift. Balance-size and statement-due-date targeting, both named by the business as likely to matter, cannot be built into this entry today — that gap is stated plainly below, not glossed over.
Approach
  • Entry on EMI_STATUS_CHANGED where New Status=Pending, Source=OS-to-EMI, Product Type=Outstanding — this is the event where a request already exists but hasn't converted, matching the user's own success definition. Rests on tool data (EMI Request attribute values) and my inference about funnel stage (assumption, since q1-1 went unanswered twice).
  • Goal on EMI_STATUS_CHANGED where New Status=Successful (same Source/Product Type) — the event that proves the behaviour. Rests on tool data.
  • Both EMI Events and Transaction Events categories are marked 'new-proposed, not confirmed built in production' by the platform itself. This entire entry+goal mechanism depends on that category going live — stated as a limitation, not presented as verified.
  • First-touch message is split 50/50 into cost-clarity vs. simplicity framing to test the user's stated-but-unconfirmed interest-cost belief against a competing explanation, changing only that one variable (my recommendation, P-005).
  • Urgency is anchored to the EMI request's own 7-day expiry clock (P-003), not the statement due date the user mentioned — Statement Due Date lives on the Account entity and is not reachable from an entry filtered on EMI Request, so this is a substitution I'm naming explicitly, not a silent swap.
  • Channel order leads with EMAIL (lowest cost) for the first touch and escalates to SMS then WHATSAPP for reminders, per the stated preference to lead low-cost and reserve higher-cost channels for reinforcement (P-010, tenant preference).
  • 10% control holdout, per the tenant's stated preferred control percentage, because any read of 'did the experiment arm do better' needs a baseline (P-006).
Options weighed
  • Segmentation — cannot evaluate yet. The business-relevant segment (outstanding balance >₹25,000) cannot be evaluated for use because the entry entity (EMI Request) carries no amount attribute; would need a verified account/running-balance attribute to decide if it's worth a separate treatment.
  • Experimentation — used. A/B on first-touch framing (cost-clarity vs. simplicity) to test the stated interest-cost belief against a competing explanation, with a holdout to separate any effect from normal expiry behaviour.
  • Conditional branching — not applicable here. The only branchable signal the builder exposes is a previous send's delivery outcome, not EMI status; the goal check already removes converters automatically, so there's no further meaningful branch to add on top of the experiment arms.
  • Channel fallback — not applicable here. The builder cannot express a fallback channel on a send (per the stated limitation); each send uses a single channel and if it fails, the sequence simply continues to the next scheduled step.
  • Adaptive sequencing — used. Channel escalates from EMAIL to SMS to WHATSAPP as the request ages toward its 7-day expiry, treating later reminders as higher-salience recovery attempts (P-010).
  • Cost and fatigue — used. Capped at 4 sends (the tenant max). The weakest message is the final 'outcome' nudge sent after the waitForEvent timeout — it can't be worded differently for 'still open' vs. 'expired' customers because the builder can't branch on EMI status, so it's a generic catch-all. Kept because it's the last chance to recover anyone who hasn't converted, even if its framing is necessarily blunt.
  • Measurement and learning — used. With the control holdout and the framing experiment, the campaign can report a genuine comparison (arm vs. arm, entrants vs. holdout) rather than only a before/after count, though still without any historical baseline to size an expected effect against.
Considered and not used
  • A separate pre-request 'you're eligible, start now' awareness track using Transaction (EMI Eligible=true, Amount>25,000) as entry — This targets a materially different behaviour (initiating a request, not completing one) and the available attribute (a single transaction's amount/eligibility) is not the same thing as 'an outstanding balance over ₹25,000' — using it would quietly change who the business thinks it's reaching. I'm flagging it as a live option for the user to greenlight separately, not building it silently alongside this one.
Success criteria
  • Business's own measure, no fixed numeric target: more EMI Requests reaching 'Successful' status (their words, confirmed).
Measurement
  • Track EMI Request New Status transitions (Pending → Successful / Failed / Expired / Cancelled) for journey entrants, split by first-touch arm (cost-clarity vs. simplicity) and against the 10% control holdout.
  • Track delivery status per channel per step (EMAIL/SMS/WHATSAPP) to see where messages aren't landing at all, separate from whether they convert.
  • To measure this properly would need: confirmation that EMI_STATUS_CHANGED (and Transaction Events) are actually live in production rather than proposed, and a decision from the business on what 'eligible base' a conversion rate should be read against if a rate (not just a count) is ever wanted.
Assumptions
  • Targeting Pending OS-to-EMI requests (not pre-request eligibility) is the primary track, inferred from the success measure given — not explicitly confirmed by the user.
  • Urgency messaging is anchored to the request's 7-day expiry clock rather than the statement due date, because the due date isn't reachable from this entry's entity.
  • No balance-based segmentation is applied; all Pending OS-to-EMI entrants are treated the same regardless of amount.
Hypotheses for future testing
  • A cost-clarity framing (showing the fixed EMI and total payable up front) will convert Pending requests to Successful at a different rate than a simplicity/ease framing — untested, to be read only against the control holdout and against each other, not against any historical benchmark.
Defaults applied
  • Is SMS acceptable as the channel for the final wrap-up message, or is a cheaper (EMAIL) or more visible (WHATSAPP) channel preferred for that last touch? Minor cost/visibility trade-off on the lowest-stakes message in the sequence. Until then: Default to SMS.
Limitations
  • EMI Events is marked new in the platform metadata: proposed, not confirmed as built in production. This campaign depends on it, so it cannot be presented as a verified platform capability.
  • Both EMI_STATUS_CHANGED and Transaction events are marked 'new — proposed, not confirmed built in production.' Can this be confirmed live before launch? The entire entry and goal for this campaign depend on this event category; if it isn't live, neither can fire.
  • The outstanding-balance-size hunch (>₹25,000) and the statement-due-date urgency hunch cannot be used for targeting or timing in this build, because the entry entity (EMI Request) has no amount or due-date attribute reachable here. Does the business want to pursue making that data available to the builder? Without it, this campaign can't test or act on either hunch, even though both were named as likely drivers.
  • The final message can't be conditioned on whether the request actually expired versus is still unresolved, because the builder's condition step only reads a previous send's delivery outcome, not EMI status. The last message has to be worded generically to work for both cases, which is weaker than a status-specific message would be.

OS-to-EMI: Convert Pending Requests to Successful · control 10%

Targets customers with a Pending OS-to-EMI (outstanding-balance-to-EMI) request and nudges them to complete it before the 7-day expiry, testing a cost-clarity vs. simplicity message framing against a control holdout.

entry: {"kind": "event", "eventCategory": "EMI Events", "eventType": "EMI_STATUS_CHANGED", "conditions": [{"attribute": "New Status", "operator": "Equals", "value": "Pending"}, {"attribute": "Source", "operator": "Equals", "value": "OS-to-EMI"}, {"attribute": "Product Type", "operator": "Equals", "value": "Outstanding"}]}
goal : {"eventCategory": "EMI Events", "eventType": "EMI_STATUS_CHANGED", "conditions": [{"attribute": "New Status", "operator": "Equals", "value": "Successful"}, {"attribute": "Source", "operator": "Equals", "value": "OS-to-EMI"}, {"attribute": "Product Type", "operator": "Equals", "value": "Outstanding"}]}
  1. EXPERIMENT
On screenawaiting-confirmation178.8s
You
On your earlier question: it's the other one. Target customers who have an eligible outstanding balance but have never raised an OS-to-EMI request at all.
Agent
Target customers who had an eligible transaction but have never raised an OS-to-EMI request, and nudge them to start and complete one before interest accrues further. The opening and follow-up messages are framed two ways — cost-clarity vs. simplicity — to test the user's interest-cost hunch against a competing explanation, with a 10% control holdout so any difference isn't mistaken for proof. Balance-size and statement-due-date targeting remain unbuildable on this entry and are flagged, not substituted.
Approach
  • Entry on Transaction Events (EMI Eligible=true, Transaction Status=SETTLED) — this is the moment the opportunity appears and the behaviour has not happened yet. Rests on tool data (Transaction entity attributes); category is marked 'new-proposed, not confirmed built in production.'
  • Goal on EMI_STATUS_CHANGED, New Status=Successful, Source=OS-to-EMI, Product Type=Outstanding — the event that proves the behaviour, regardless of how many messages it took. Rests on tool data; same production-readiness caveat applies.
  • First-touch and reminder copy A/B'd on cost-clarity vs. simplicity framing to test the user's stated-but-unconfirmed interest-cost belief against a competing explanation (unawareness/flow friction), changing one variable consistently per arm (P-005, my recommendation).
  • A waitForEvent on EMI_STATUS_CHANGED New Status=Pending is used mid-sequence as a soft timing checkpoint (not a branch — the builder can't branch on it), so the final message arrives after customers have had a real window to start a request, whether or not they did.
  • Channel order leads with EMAIL (lowest cost) for first-touch, escalates to SMS then WHATSAPP for reminders, per stated preference to lead low-cost and reserve higher-cost channels for reinforcement (P-010).
  • 10% control holdout, per the tenant's stated preferred control percentage, because any read of 'did the framing help' needs a baseline (P-006).
Options weighed
  • Segmentation — cannot evaluate yet. The business-relevant segment (outstanding balance >₹25,000) can't be evaluated for use: the entry entity (Transaction) only exposes a single transaction's amount, not an account-level outstanding balance. Would need a verified account-level balance attribute to decide if it's worth a separate treatment.
  • Experimentation — used. A/B on framing (cost-clarity vs. simplicity) across the whole sequence per arm, to test the user's stated belief against a real competing explanation, read against the control holdout.
  • Conditional branching — not applicable here. The only branchable signal is a previous send's delivery outcome, not EMI status; goal check already removes converters automatically, so there's nothing further to branch on.
  • Channel fallback — not applicable here. The builder cannot express a fallback channel on a send; if a send fails, the sequence simply continues to its next scheduled step.
  • Adaptive sequencing — used. Channel escalates from EMAIL to SMS to WHATSAPP as the opportunity ages, and a waitForEvent checkpoint lets the final message land after a realistic window for the customer to have started a request.
  • Cost and fatigue — used. Capped at 3 sends (under the tenant max of 4). The weakest message is the final WHATSAPP nudge — it can't be worded differently for 'already started' vs. 'still hasn't acted' because the builder can't branch on EMI status, so it's necessarily generic. Kept because it's the last chance to recover anyone still eligible, even with blunter framing.
  • Measurement and learning — used. With the control holdout and the framing experiment, the campaign can report a genuine arm-vs-arm and arm-vs-holdout comparison, though still without any historical baseline to size an expected effect against.
Considered and not used
  • Real-time point-of-sale nudge (push/in-app prompt at the moment the eligible transaction settles) instead of a scheduled multi-day drip — Would likely reach customers at a higher-intent moment, but needs real-time checkout/app integration this discovery hasn't evidenced as available, and would still need the same unresolved balance/due-date data to target well. Recommending the drip because it fits the confirmed tooling; flagging the real-time option as a materially different mechanism worth separate evaluation.
  • Running the requested-but-incomplete (Pending) track as part of this same campaign — That is a different behaviour (completing vs. starting) with a different entry event and urgency clock (7-day request expiry vs. no defined eligibility window). Keeping it as a separate campaign rather than merging two audiences with different needs into one journey.
Success criteria
  • Business's own measure, no fixed numeric target: more EMI Requests reaching 'Successful' status (their words, confirmed).
Measurement
  • Track entrants' EMI Request New Status transitions (none → Pending → Successful/Failed/Expired/Cancelled), split by framing arm (cost-clarity vs. simplicity) and against the 10% control holdout.
  • Track delivery status per channel per step (EMAIL/SMS/WHATSAPP) to separate 'didn't land' from 'landed but didn't convert.'
  • To measure this properly would need: confirmation that Transaction Events and EMI Events are actually live in production rather than proposed, and a defined 'eligible base' denominator if the business ever wants a rate rather than a count.
Assumptions
  • An eligible transaction's actionable window is assumed to be roughly 7 days (symmetric with the 7-day EMI request expiry rule, P-003) — no confirmed eligibility-expiry rule exists for Transaction-level EMI eligibility, so sequencing is sized to this assumption.
  • Transaction Status=SETTLED is used as the entry filter (a completed, non-reversed purchase) rather than APPROVED, to avoid messaging on transactions that may still reverse.
  • No balance-based segmentation is applied; all eligible, never-requested entrants are treated the same regardless of transaction amount.
Hypotheses for future testing
  • A cost-clarity framing (fixed EMI amount, total payable shown upfront) will produce a different request-start/completion rate than a simplicity/ease framing — untested, to be read only against the control holdout and against the other arm, not against any historical benchmark.
Worth settling before this is built
  • Balance-size and statement-due-date targeting were both named as likely drivers but neither is reachable from the Transaction entry used here. Is it worth pursuing a build change (exposing account-level outstanding balance and statement due date as entry-joinable attributes) so these hunches can actually be tested? Without this, the campaign can never confirm or refute either hunch — it stays untestable indefinitely, not just unbuilt this time. Until then: Proceed without balance or due-date targeting; treat both as open hypotheses for future platform work, not as something this build quietly approximates.
Defaults applied
  • Is SMS acceptable as the mid-sequence reminder channel, or is a different channel preferred for that step? Minor cost/visibility trade-off on a middle-priority message. Until then: Default to SMS, consistent with leading low-cost and reserving WHATSAPP for the final recovery touch (P-010).
Limitations
  • Transaction Events is marked new in the platform metadata: proposed, not confirmed as built in production. This campaign depends on it, so it cannot be presented as a verified platform capability.
  • EMI Events is marked new in the platform metadata: proposed, not confirmed as built in production. This campaign depends on it, so it cannot be presented as a verified platform capability.
  • Entry on an eligible Transaction cannot exclude customers who already have an open OS-to-EMI request or who already converted on a different balance, because the builder can only filter conditions on one entity at entry. Is this an acceptable risk, or should the eligible-transaction population be narrowed some other way before this campaign launches? Without this, some entrants may receive 'you haven't started yet' messaging despite already being mid-request or already converted elsewhere — a real relevance/annoyance risk, not just a targeting inefficiency.

Targets customers with a settled, EMI-eligible transaction who have never raised an OS-to-EMI request, and encourages them to start and complete one. Tests a cost-clarity vs. simplicity message framing against a control holdout, since the stated interest-cost barrier is an unconfirmed hypothesis.

I now understand the goal is to get dormant credit cards transacting again. Before I design the audience, the entry point and the message sequence, I need three things settled: how you yourselves will judge whether this worked, what 'dormant' means in practice (since the platform can only target what an event or attribute actually records), and your working theory of why these customers stopped — because that changes whether the message should sell a benefit, remove a blocker, or just remind. A drip campaign is the right instrument here, but these answers change who enters it and what it says, so I'm asking before proposing rather than guessing a definition on your behalf.

On screenawaiting-confirmation215.0s
You
Success is simply any transaction after we re-engage them. Dormant means no transaction in 6 months. We think they've just forgotten about the card.
Agent
Enter customers whose account is flagged Dormant and send a short reminder sequence, capped at 3 of the allowed 4 messages, escalating from the cheapest channel (EMAIL) to SMS to WhatsApp. Because the bank's cause theory ('they forgot') is a belief not a fact, the opening message is A/B tested against a benefit-led alternative, with a 10% holdout so any read is not confounded with normal background reactivation. The goal is any customer-initiated transaction after entry, which auto-exits converters per platform behaviour.
Approach
  • Entry = Account.Status Equals 'Dormant' (tool: confirmed allowed value on Account entity) — this is the only buildable proxy for the user's 6-month no-transaction definition; it is not verified to use the same threshold, which is flagged as an open item rather than silently assumed equal.
  • Goal = Transaction event, Initiated By = CUSTOMER_INITIATED (assumption: excludes system-generated fees/reversals/interest postings so the goal reflects genuine customer activity, matching the user's 'any transaction' intent as closely as the schema allows). Transaction Events are marked new/proposed in platform metadata — flagged as an operational limitation, not presented as verified.
  • Experiment used instead of a single message because the user's 'forgot' explanation is a belief, not a finding (user-belief), and a single-variable test (P-005) can tell plain-reminder and benefit-led messaging apart without extra campaigns.
  • Channel order EMAIL → SMS → WHATSAPP follows the tenant's stated preference to lead with the lower-cost channel (P-010) and keeps the highest-cost channel for the final, highest-stakes touch.
  • Message count held to 3 of the available 4 (assumption, conservative choice) in line with the tenant's stated preference for fewer, better-targeted messages over broad reach.
  • A condition on the first send's delivery outcome is used to approximate channel fallback, since a native fallback-on-send field does not exist in this builder (capability gap, handled via the closest supported mechanism).
Options weighed
  • Segmentation — not applicable here. User explicitly described one undifferentiated dormant group with no severity bands; no other dimension surfaced that warrants a different treatment at this stage.
  • Experimentation — used. Tests the user's 'forgot' belief against a competing 'benefit-salience' explanation by varying only the opening message's content between two arms, with a 10% holdout to separate any effect from background reactivation.
  • Conditional branching — used. Branches on the first send's delivery outcome (DELIVERED vs not) to decide whether the next touch is a reinforcement or a same-content resend on a different channel.
  • Channel fallback — used. No native fallback-on-send field exists in this builder; implemented via the delivery-outcome condition instead, which is the closest supported mechanism — flagged as a workaround, not the real feature.
  • Adaptive sequencing — used. Channel escalates from cheapest (EMAIL) to SMS to WhatsApp as the sequence progresses, consistent with P-010; no timing escalation beyond minimum spacing since the opportunity does not have a hard expiry.
  • Cost and fatigue — used. Capped at 3 of 4 allowed messages. The final WhatsApp message is the weakest link — a customer who hasn't responded to two prior touches is less likely to convert on a third — but it is kept because it is the last remaining low-cost-relative touch within the cap and the min-spacing window has already elapsed, so the marginal cost of trying is small.
  • Measurement and learning — used. The 10% holdout lets the 90% treated population be compared against a baseline that received no message; this can show a directional difference but, per the brief, cannot be reported as caused lift without a randomised read and without historical baselines, which don't exist for this bank.
Considered and not used
  • Lead with fixing structural blockers (never-activated, locked or blocked cards) instead of a reminder campaign — The user's stated theory is simple forgetting, not blockage, so this is not the approach they asked for. However, the builder cannot filter Card attributes (Locked/Blocked/Is Ever Activated) at this entry because only one entity's conditions are usable at entry and Account is already used for dormancy — so some entered customers may hold structurally blocked cards that no reminder can fix. This is carried forward as a known limitation, not silently designed around.
Success criteria
  • The business's own measure: any transaction by a dormant cardholder after they are re-engaged by this campaign.
  • Directionally, a rise in the share of entered dormant accounts that transact again, read against the 10% holdout — not against a fixed target, since no historical baseline exists for this bank.
Measurement
  • Track customer-initiated Transaction events per entered customer, comparing the 90% treated population against the 10% control holdout to see whether transacting-again is more common when messaged.
  • Within the treated population, compare Arm A (plain reminder) against Arm B (benefit-led message) to read whether 'forgot' or 'benefit salience' better explains the dormancy — a hypothesis comparison, not a performance claim.
  • To measure this properly: confirm Transaction Events are actually live in production (currently marked new/proposed in platform metadata) and agree a fixed reporting window (e.g. 30 or 60 days post-entry) before reading any result.
Assumptions
  • Account.Status = 'Dormant' is treated as the nearest buildable proxy for 'no transaction in 6 months' — not confirmed to use the same threshold.
  • A 'transaction' for goal purposes means customer-initiated activity, excluding system-generated fees, interest and reversals.
  • Quiet hours, DNC and NPA exclusions are enforced automatically by the platform's existing guardrails and do not need to be encoded in this journey.
Hypotheses for future testing
  • Dormant cardholders will respond to a plain reminder because they simply forgot the card exists, as the bank believes.
  • A benefit-led reminder (e.g. surfacing rewards) may outperform a plain reminder if the real blocker is benefit visibility rather than memory — the competing explanation this experiment is designed to separate out.
Worth settling before this is built
  • Does the platform's Account.Status = 'Dormant' reflect your 6-month no-transaction definition, and does it apply at account level or per-card when a customer holds multiple cards? Determines whether the entry population actually matches the group you described, or is broader or narrower than intended. Until then: Proceed using Account.Status = Dormant as the entry audience, explicitly flagged as an approximation rather than a verified match to your 6-month definition.
Defaults applied
  • Confirm the control group size for the holdout. Affects how much of the audience is withheld versus messaged, and the statistical sharpness of any later comparison. Until then: Default to the tenant's stated preference of 10%.
Limitations
  • Transaction Events is marked new in the platform metadata: proposed, not confirmed as built in production. This campaign depends on it, so it cannot be presented as a verified platform capability.
  • Transaction Events (used for the goal) are marked 'new — proposed' in the platform metadata, not confirmed built in production. If Transaction events are not actually live, the goal cannot be detected, and the automatic 'goal reached' exit will never fire for converters.
  • The builder only allows one entity's conditions at entry, so blocked, locked or never-activated cards inside the Dormant population can't be excluded even though a reminder message cannot reactivate them. Part of the entered audience may be structurally incapable of transacting, which would understate the message's real effect when results are read.
Cannot be generated yet

Still unknown
  • Whether the bank's internal 'Dormant' account-status threshold is exactly 6 months or some other window.
  • Whether blocked, locked or never-activated cards sit inside the Dormant population — these can't be excluded at entry because the builder allows only one entity's conditions per entry, and Account conditions can't be combined with Card conditions.
  • Whether Transaction Events (the goal) are confirmed live in production — currently flagged new/proposed in the platform metadata.

Whether you mean a fixed no-spend window (e.g. 90 days, 6 months) and whether recently-dormant and long-dormant customers should get different treatment changes both the entry mapping and whether one journey or several are needed.
    note Dormancy = no transaction in 6 months, treated as one undifferentiated group (user did not ask for severity bands). The platform's nearest buildable attribute is Account.Status = 'Dormant', which is a bank-set status flag, not a computed 'months since last transaction' figure — its exact threshold is not confirmed to equal 6 months. Flagged as an open item rather than assumed equivalent.
  • retaineduser-belief believed cause of dormancy
    why Reactivation messaging differs a lot depending on the reason: forgot the card exists, dissatisfied with rewards/fees, switched spend to another card or payment method, or the physical/virtual card itself is blocked or was never activated. This decides the message's core argument, not just its wording.
    note User believes customers simply forgot about the card. This is an unverified belief about cause, not a confirmed finding. Rather than designing solely around it, it is pitted against a competing explanation (benefit salience) in a controlled A/B test, since the user cannot actually know which is true and testing is the honest way to close a stated cause. This is the user's own explanation, carried as a hypothesis: it has not been tested and competing explanations may remain.
Success criteria
  • The business's own measure: any transaction by a dormant cardholder after they are re-engaged by this campaign.
  • Directionally, a rise in the share of entered dormant accounts that transact again, read against the 10% holdout — not against a fixed target, since no historical baseline exists for this bank.

On screenawaiting-confirmation266.0s
You
No fixed conversion-rate target. Success is more EMI Requests reaching Successful. Our hunch is that outstanding balances above 25,000 rupees convert better, and that urgency rises near the statement due date. We think interest-cost hesitation is the barrier.
Agent
Enter customers the moment an EMI_STATUS_CHANGED event shows an OS-to-EMI request in Pending status, and work to get that specific request to Successful before it expires at 7 days. The opening message tests the user's interest-cost hypothesis against a plain urgency message (A/B), escalates channel cost as the window ages, and recovers non-delivered opens via an alternate channel. A 10% control is held out so any difference can be read against a genuine no-contact baseline, not just reported as 'what happened'.
Approach
  • Entry on EMI_STATUS_CHANGED, New Status = Pending, Source = OS-to-EMI — chosen because it is the only buildable event that proves 'a request now exists and is not yet resolved'; relies on tool data (list_event_types, list_audience_attributes). Limitation: this event category is marked new/proposed, not confirmed live.
  • Goal on EMI_STATUS_CHANGED, New Status = Successful, Source = OS-to-EMI — matches the user's own success definition exactly (basis: user).
  • No audience filter on outstanding balance size — basis: tool (no such attribute exists); the user's >₹25,000 hunch is preserved as an open hypothesis, not quietly dropped or proxied.
  • First-touch message is A/B split between cost-reassurance framing and urgency-only framing — basis: user-belief needs testing, not assuming; my own judgement on how to test it.
  • Channel order EMAIL → SMS → WHATSAPP, cheapest first, escalating as the 7-day window ages — basis: tenant preference (P-010, 'prefer lower-cost channel first') and my judgement on pacing against the expiry.
  • 10% control group — basis: tenant default preference stated in the brief (conservative risk appetite, explicit control group), applied as a default since the user did not override it.
Options weighed
  • Segmentation — cannot evaluate yet. The one segmentation the business actually hypothesised (balance above ₹25,000) has no supporting attribute today; nothing else in the data suggests a different group needs different treatment. Would need an outstanding-balance field exposed to the builder to evaluate properly.
  • Experimentation — used. Cost-reassurance vs urgency-only first-touch framing, read by comparing the proportion of each arm reaching Successful, against the 10% control. This directly tests the user's stated cause rather than assuming it.
  • Conditional branching — used. Branch on whether the first-touch send actually delivered, so a non-delivered customer is reached through a different channel rather than silently dropped.
  • Channel fallback — used. Built via the supported condition-on-delivery-outcome primitive, not a native fallback field — the builder has no per-send fallback property, so this is the closest substitute and is labelled as such.
  • Adaptive sequencing — used. Channel escalates EMAIL → SMS → WHATSAPP as the request ages toward its 7-day expiry, and the final message's tone shifts to closing urgency.
  • Cost and fatigue — used. Capped at 3 sends per customer path (within the 4-message cap), each 48h apart. Weakest message is the mid-sequence reminder/recovery send — it's the most generic one, kept because it's needed either to reinforce the opening message or to recover a non-delivered one, not because it's expected to do much alone.
  • Measurement and learning — used. With a randomised 10% control and two framing arms, the campaign can report an associational difference between arms and against the control. Without that control, nothing here could be called caused by the campaign — this is why the control is kept despite the conservative risk appetite favouring fewer messages.
Considered and not used
  • Single linear sequence with no delivery-outcome branching — Simpler, but a non-delivered first message would silently drop the customer with no recovery attempt inside a hard 7-day window. The added condition step is low-cost and directly serves a time-critical goal, so it was kept instead.
  • Route high-value Pending requests to a relationship-manager/agent outreach instead of automated messaging — A materially different approach — a human-assisted channel rather than a drip. Not pursued here because no such channel exists in this platform and the user asked for a drip campaign; flagged so the user can pursue it separately if the automated approach underperforms their expectations, especially for the balances they believe matter most.
Success criteria
  • More EMI Requests (Source = OS-to-EMI) reaching New Status = Successful — the business's own measure, no numeric target set.
Measurement
  • Track, per arm (cost-reassurance / urgency-only / control), the count and share of entrants whose EMI Request reaches Successful vs Failed/Expired/Cancelled within the 7-day window.
  • Read the A/B difference as a directional signal on the interest-cost hypothesis only, since it is a message-framing comparison, not a segment comparison.
  • Read the control-vs-treated difference as the only basis for any causal claim (P-006); without it, results are description, not attribution.
  • To properly test the balance-size hunch later, the business would need an outstanding-balance attribute exposed to the builder — currently absent.
Assumptions
  • EMI_STATUS_CHANGED firing on both Pending and Successful (and Source = OS-to-EMI being populated) works as described, pending production confirmation since it is marked new/proposed.
  • Quiet hours (21:00–09:00) and the 48h minimum spacing are enforced by the platform automatically; design respects them but cannot add time-of-day logic itself.
  • 10% control and cheapest-channel-first ordering are applied as tenant defaults since the user did not specify otherwise this round.
Hypotheses for future testing
  • Reassuring customers about fixed, predictable EMI cost in the first message will move more Pending OS-to-EMI requests to Successful than a plain urgency message — untested, worth the A/B.
  • Escalating to a higher-cost channel only as expiry nears will recover some requests that would otherwise lapse — untested.
Defaults applied
  • Keep the tenant's default 10% control group and cheapest-channel-first ordering (EMAIL → SMS → WHATSAPP)? Affects how cleanly any later read of the A/B/control can be attributed, and the cost profile of the sequence. Until then: Keep both defaults as proposed.
Limitations
  • EMI Events is marked new in the platform metadata: proposed, not confirmed as built in production. This campaign depends on it, so it cannot be presented as a verified platform capability.
  • EMI_STATUS_CHANGED (used for both entry and goal) is marked new/proposed, not confirmed built in production. Can this be confirmed before launch? If this event isn't actually live, neither entry nor goal will fire and the campaign cannot run as designed.
  • No Account or EMI Request attribute exposes an outstanding-balance amount, so the >₹25,000 segment and the 'eligible but not yet started' audience cannot be built. Without it, the user's stated hunch about balance size can't be targeted or tested, and the bigger-opportunity audience (never started a request) is unreachable by this campaign.
Cannot be generated yet
  • steps[0].experiment: Experiment arm percentages sum to 90, not 100.
Still unknown
  • Whether the user wants a separate effort (once buildable) to reach customers with an eligible outstanding balance who have not yet started any EMI request — left open, not decided on their behalf.
  • Whether interest-cost hesitation, once tested, turns out to be the real barrier versus unawareness or mid-flow drop-off — this is exactly what the A/B is for.
  • Whether balances above ₹25,000 genuinely convert better — cannot be measured or targeted without a new attribute.
Generate this campaign?

Nothing has been built yet. Confirm to create the journey, or tell the agent what to change.

Before I design a dormant-card reactivation journey I need two things settled: how the business will judge success (this is explicitly theirs to give, not mine to assume), and what 'dormant' actually means operationally — because the platform exposes several different signals (Account.Status=Dormant, Card.Status Active/Inactive, Is Ever Activated, and raw Transaction recency) that point at materially different populations and would lead to different entry logic and messaging. I also want to check your working theory of why these customers stopped, since that changes the intervention (a reminder nudge vs. a value/incentive message vs. a limit or fee reassurance). I've checked what events, attributes and channels the platform actually supports so my questions stay inside what's real, and confirmed the template library itself isn't readable from here, so I'll draft copy rather than reference a template id.
1How will you judge whether this campaign worked — e.g. a rise in transacting-card rate, a specific number of reactivated cards, or something else? If you don't have a number yet, that's fine, just say so.
2When you say 'dormant' / 'stopped transacting months ago', which group do you mean: (a) accounts the bank's own system already flags as Account Status = Dormant, (b) cards that are still Active but have had no transactions for some period (e.g. 3+ months), or (c) cards that were issued but never activated at all? These are different populations in the data and lead to different entry criteria.
3What's your working theory for why these customers stopped transacting — e.g. they forgot about the card, another card became their default, a fee/rate concern, or a card access problem (lost/blocked)? If you're not sure, I'll treat this as unknown and consider testing a couple of angles instead of guessing.

You
No incentive available right now, it has to be a plain reminder. And treat everyone the same, we don't have value tiers to hand.
Agent
A single-treatment, plain-reminder drip for accounts flagged Dormant, nudging holders that their card still works, with no incentive and no urgency framing per the user's instruction. Entry uses the bank's categorical Dormant flag as the closest buildable proxy for the user's '6 months no transaction' definition, a gap we flag rather than silently close. Three spaced, escalating-channel reminders run inside the 4-message cap, with a 10% holdout so the business can read a treatment-vs-control contrast rather than raw before/after.
Approach
  • Entry population: Account.Status Equals 'Dormant' (tool: list_audience_attributes) — chosen because the builder accepts only one entity's attributes per audience entry, and no entity exposes a recency/'months since last transaction' field. This is a proxy for the user's stated definition, not an exact match; the difference is surfaced as a limitation below, not hidden.
  • No never-activated cards excluded explicitly at entry because doing so would require a second entity's attributes (Card.Is Ever Activated), which the single-entity audience entry cannot combine with Account.Status (tool: builder capability notes). Flagged as a known population-purity gap, not solved by substituting a different attribute.
  • Goal: a customer-initiated, approved/settled Transaction event after entry (tool: list_event_types, list_audience_attributes) — this is the direct proof the behaviour happened. Noted as 'new-proposed', not confirmed live in production, per the tool's own status flag.
  • No incentive, no urgency, identical treatment for all entrants (user, confirmed twice) — message content is a plain, low-pressure reminder surfacing the card's continued usability.
  • Channel order EMAIL → SMS → WHATSAPP, cheapest-first escalating to richer/more attention-getting channels for later reminders (tenant preference: prefer lower-cost channel first; principle P-010).
  • 3 of the 4 allowed sends used, spaced 96 hours apart (above the 48-hour minimum) to reduce fatigue (principle P-011) and to match the conservative, 'fewer better-targeted messages' risk appetite rather than maxing out the cap.
  • 10% control group held out (tenant preference: 10%) so the business can read a treatment-vs-control contrast; without it, any observed change cannot be separated from what would have happened anyway (principle P-006).
Options weighed
  • Segmentation — not applicable here. User confirmed uniform treatment and no value-tier data exists; nothing in the dimensions found a split that would change the message or channel for this population.
  • Experimentation — used. A 10% holdout is built to let the business compare exposed vs. unexposed reactivation, since no incentive variant exists to A/B test against the plain reminder; a future copy- or channel-angle test is noted as a hypothesis, not built now.
  • Conditional branching — not applicable here. The only meaningful branch — goal achieved — is already handled automatically by the platform's goal-check/exit; there is no second decision point in a single plain-reminder treatment.
  • Channel fallback — cannot evaluate yet. The builder has no fallback-channel field on a send; a delivery-outcome condition step could reroute but would add a branch disproportionate to a 3-message plain reminder. Raised as a limitation rather than built.
  • Adaptive sequencing — used. Channel escalates EMAIL → SMS → WHATSAPP as reminders progress, from cheapest to more attention-getting, per P-010.
  • Cost and fatigue — used. Capped at 3 of 4 allowed sends, 96 hours apart. The third (WhatsApp) reminder is the weakest: anyone unmoved by two prior identical-intent nudges is less likely to convert on a third, but it's kept because it's a cheap, different-medium touch still inside the cap — a deliberate trade-off, not a clear win.
  • Measurement and learning — used. The control group gives a genuine treatment-vs-no-treatment read. Beyond that single contrast, this plain reminder sequence doesn't isolate which message or channel drove any change — that would need a further, separately varied test.
Considered and not used
  • Incentive-led reactivation (cashback/fee waiver on next spend) — Explicitly rejected by the user — no incentive available right now. Carried as a hypothesis worth testing once one exists, not designed around.
  • Tiered treatment by value/credit limit — User confirmed uniform treatment, and the platform has no value-tier attribute to target with anyway, so this was not a live option even before the user's answer.
  • Agent-assisted outbound call for highest-value dormant holders — A materially different, non-drip mechanism; set aside because the ask was specifically for a drip campaign and there is no tier data to decide who would qualify for it.
Success criteria
  • Business-stated measure: more dormant cards transacting again, judged qualitatively — no specific number or rate target was given.
Measurement
  • Track: Transaction goal completions (customer-initiated, approved/settled) among entrants vs. the 10% control group, over the campaign window.
  • Evaluate as a simple exposed-vs-control comparison, not a raw before/after, since no history exists to compare against.
  • To measure properly: confirm Transaction Events are actually live in production (currently flagged 'new-proposed'), and ideally get a true recency field ('days/months since last transaction') added so entry can match the user's 6-month definition instead of the categorical Dormant flag.
Assumptions
  • Account.Status = Dormant is an acceptable, if imperfect, stand-in for 'no transaction in 6 months' until a recency attribute exists.
  • 96-hour spacing between reminders is a reasonable default balancing reach against fatigue; no data exists to tune this.
  • DNC and NPA exclusions and quiet-hours scheduling are applied automatically by the tenant's standing guardrails, not set explicitly in this blueprint's conditions.
Hypotheses for future testing
  • A plain reminder that simply resurfaces the card (no incentive) will move some forgetting-driven dormant holders to transact again — untested.
  • If this plain reminder shows limited movement in the control contrast, an incentive-attached or urgency-framed variant would likely need testing against it to isolate what the dormancy is actually driven by (forgetting vs. cost/access/preference reasons).
Worth settling before this is built
  • Is Account.Status = Dormant (the bank's categorical flag) an acceptable stand-in for your '6 months since last transaction' definition, given its exact threshold isn't verified and it may include accounts dormant for reasons other than pure transaction recency? It decides who actually enters the campaign — a materially different population if the bank's Dormant threshold differs from 6 months. Until then: Proceed using Account.Status = Dormant as the closest available proxy, explicitly flagged as not an exact match.
Defaults applied
  • Is 96 hours between reminders (3 sends total, inside the 4-message cap) the right cadence, or would you prefer faster/slower spacing? Affects total fatigue and how quickly the sequence completes. Until then: Default to 96-hour spacing, 3 of 4 allowed sends.
  • Keep the tenant's default 10% control group for this campaign? Determines whether a treatment-vs-control read is possible at all. Until then: Default to 10% control, per tenant preference.
Limitations
  • Transaction Events is marked new in the platform metadata: proposed, not confirmed as built in production. This campaign depends on it, so it cannot be presented as a verified platform capability.
  • Transaction Events (used for the goal) and Card Events are marked 'new-proposed' — not confirmed live in production. Can this be confirmed before launch? If the goal event isn't actually firing, reactivation will never be detected and customers won't exit the journey early even after converting.
Still unknown
  • Whether Account.Status=Dormant's internal threshold is close to 6 months of no transactions, or materially different.
  • Whether the Transaction Events category will be confirmed live before this campaign would need to run.
  • Whether holders in Dormant status include never-activated cards, which the single-entity entry condition cannot exclude.

Dormant Card Reactivation — Plain Reminder · control 10%

Three-touch, cheapest-channel-first reminder sequence for accounts flagged Dormant, with no incentive and uniform treatment, built to surface a forgotten card rather than create urgency. Includes a 10% holdout for a treatment-vs-control read.

entry: {"kind": "audience", "entity": "Account", "conditions": [{"attribute": "Status", "operator": "Equals", "value": "Dormant"}]}
goal : {"eventCategory": "Transaction Events", "eventType": "Transaction", "conditions": [{"attribute": "Transaction Status", "operator": "Any of", "value": ["APPROVED", "SETTLED"]}, {"attribute": "Initiated By", "operator": "Equals", "value": "CUSTOMER_INITIATED"}]}
  1. SEND First reminder EMAIL
    Hi ${customerFirstName}, we noticed your IndusInd card hasn't been used in a while. It's still active and ready whenever you need it.
    cta View my card
  2. WAIT 96h
    Space reminders well above the 48-hour minimum to avoid fatigue, per conservative messaging preference.
  3. SEND Second reminder SMS
    Hi ${customerFirstName}, your IndusInd card is still active. Use it for your next purchase whenever it suits you.
    cta Use my card
  4. WAIT 96h
    Maintain consistent spacing before the final reminder.
  5. SEND Third reminder WHATSAPP
    Hi ${customerFirstName}, many customers use their IndusInd card for everyday spends like groceries, bills and online shopping. Yours is ready whenever you are.
    cta Start using it
  6. EXIT
    End of plain-reminder sequence; no further messages within this campaign's cap.
